attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post, said in his own voice. The thread he rebuts is quoted separately.

semantics.note: The revision puts back 'roughly speaking', 'a lot of' and 'not really all that close'. These limit degree, not probability, so this is a firm observation about systems at the time.

contract.note: Plain reading: systems stayed well below reliable human comprehension across varied situations. That is an ordinary reading of 'not all that close'. No threshold is given, so the result depends on the evaluator's reading.

evidence.note: BIG-bench preprint from June 2022 compares models to expert humans across many tasks. The best models score below 20 against roughly 100 for experts. This is partial support from a deliberately hard task set.
PaLM paper from April 2022: PaLM 540B beats the average human on BIG-bench in aggregate, though it trails on 35% of tasks. This is material counterevidence to large deficits.

reviews.rationale: The two studies from the period disagree. Against expert raters, models fall far short; against average humans, PaLM is ahead in aggregate. The contract says no single aggregate score settles general comprehension, and the packet has no robustness or contextual-interpretation evidence. The support condition is not clearly met, nor is the contradiction condition.

attribution.note: Marcus's own summary sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: Reading the claim as being about machine approaches to language acquisition matches the sentence just before it. 'Not really working' is a firm but loose evaluative observation.

contract.note: Reading 'working' as reaching general two-way language competence follows his own definition in the context, so the reading is fair. With no threshold given, the result depends on that reading.

evidence.note: February 2022 study of the COGS benchmark: seq2seq models fail structural generalization, while compositional parsers succeed. It covers one narrow semantic-parsing benchmark and shows neither general success nor general failure.
LaMDA paper from January 2022 shows dialogue metrics improving with fine-tuning. It reports progress but does not assess general language competence.

reviews.rationale: The support condition needs converging evaluations showing general failure, and the packet does not have them. Neither item shows reliable general competence either. The evidence shows failure on some parts and progress on others, so it does not settle the broad claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The normalised claim keeps his two-way definition of acquiring language and the universal 'no existing machine'. Leaving out the part about children is correct.

contract.note: His comparison with children supports reading the claim as general, human-breadth competence, so the reading is fair. A narrow engineering reading (AMR parsing and generation) would flip the result, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: March 2022 preprint: one system does both AMR parsing and AMR-to-text generation. These are narrow mappings to a formal representation. They do not show general competence, nor that it was absent.

reviews.rationale: Under the contract's general-competence reading, e6 does not contradict the claim, and nothing in the packet broadly establishes that machines at the time lacked both abilities. The packet itself notes it has no full basis for the universal negative. Neither the support condition nor the contradiction condition is met.
